title: No More U.S. Trips to Cuba? New Rules Freeze Tourism Money!
summary: Imagine planning a sunny vacation to Cuba, but suddenly, the U.S. says, 'Stop! No money can go there.' That's kind of what happened on Monday, July 13, 2026. The U.S. Treasury Department put new sanctions (rules that punish a country by cutting off business) on Cuba's Ministry of Tourism. That's the part of the government that handles visitors and hotels. They also sanctioned two huge state-owned companies: GEMAR (which moves things by sea) and GECOMEX (which handles foreign trade). So, any American company doing business with them has until August 12 to stop, or they'll get in trouble too. Why is this happening? The U.S. says Cuba is a 'national security threat.' Ambassador Mike Waltz even said Russia and China might be 'collecting information around our military bases in Cuba.' But Cuba's foreign minister, Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla, says these sanctions are 'an act of collective punishment' that hurts regular people. And it's already hurting. Because of a U.S. oil blockade (stopping fuel from getting in), Cuba has had huge blackouts. Last Friday, over 10 million people—almost the whole country—lost electricity. That was the second nationwide outage in one week! The U.S. started this blockade after it took Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Venezuela used to send Cuba most of its fuel, but not anymore. Mexico also stopped sending oil after U.S. pressure. During a UN debate, Waltz told Cuba's leaders to 'change your ways and turn the lights back on for your people.' But Parrilla said the U.S. embargoes caused $8 billion in damage in just one year. It's a big fight, and kids in Cuba are sitting in the dark.
why_it_matters: These sanctions mean that children in Cuba may have to sit in the dark because there isn't enough fuel for electricity—showing how political fights between countries can affect families and kids just like you.

background_read: Cuba is an island nation very close to the United States, just 90 miles from Florida. For decades, relations between the two countries have been tense.
In 1962, the U.S. started a trade embargo against Cuba, which meant American companies could not buy from or sell to the island. Over the years, more restrictions have been added.

The situation got even harder for Cuba after the U.S. took Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro (the leader of Venezuela, an oil-rich country in South America) in January, cutting off the fuel Venezuela used to send to Cuba.
Article_Structure: WHO: The U.S. Treasury Department and Ambassador Mike Waltz; Cuba's Ministry of Tourism and state companies GEMAR and GECOMEX; Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla
WHAT: Imposed new sanctions that freeze tourism money and give American companies until August 12 to stop doing business with the targeted Cuban groups
WHERE: The sanctions affect travel and trade between the United States and Cuba

WHY: The U.S. calls Cuba a national security threat and suspects Russia and China may be collecting information near U.S. bases; Cuba says the sanctions are collective punishment causing blackouts and everyday suffering

perspectives.description: American officials argue the sanctions are needed to protect national security and pressure Cuba to stop working with Russia and China, especially near U.S. military bases.
Cuban leaders say the sanctions are an act of collective punishment that hurt ordinary people, not just the government, and blame the embargoes for nationwide blackouts and $8 billion in damages.
Blockades often lead to shortages of medicine, food, and fuel, making life extremely difficult for families who just want to go to school and have their lights and hospitals working.
